questions.question: How do you create typed and directional channels in Go?
questions.title: Creating channels and expressing direction
questions.direct_answer: Create an initialized channel with `make(chan T)` or `make(chan T, capacity)`, where `T` is the element type. A bidirectional `chan T` can be narrowed at an API boundary to `chan<- T` for send-only or `<-chan T` for receive-only. Direction documents ownership and is checked by the compiler.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding channel type, initialization, capacity, and compile-time direction constraints.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring a channel variable but forgetting `make`, leaving a nil channel that never becomes ready.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use direction to show which function owns sending and which side returns the stream.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `make(chan T)` creates an unbuffered channel for values of type `T`.
`make(chan T, n)` creates a channel with buffer capacity `n`.
`chan T` permits send and receive; `chan<- T` only send; `<-chan T` only receive.
A bidirectional channel can be assigned to a directional channel where allowed.
Direction is an API guarantee; it does not create a second channel.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A channel is a typed communication value. I initialize one with `make`, such as `make(chan int)` for an unbuffered integer channel or `make(chan int, 3)` for capacity three. The element type controls which values may cross, and the capacity controls when communication can proceed without the other side being ready immediately.

A normal `chan int` is bidirectional. At function boundaries I narrow it to `chan<- int` when the function only sends, or `<-chan int` when it only receives. The compiler then rejects an accidental operation in the wrong direction. This is not a copy: both views refer to the same underlying channel.

For example, a producer can create a bidirectional channel, start a goroutine that owns sending and closing, and return it as `<-chan int`. The caller can range over the results but cannot send into that stream or close it through the receive-only reference.

Direction describes capability, not lifecycle by itself. The API still needs an owner for closing, a cancellation path if a receiver stops early, and a deliberate buffer size. Declaring `var ch chan int` without `make` leaves `ch` nil rather than ready for use.

sections.title: One channel, narrower capabilities
sections.content:
`make` allocates and initializes the channel state. Its element type and capacity are fixed for that channel. Assigning it to a directional variable changes what operations are permitted through that variable, not the channel's storage, identity, or behaviour.

This makes direction useful for design. A producer returning `<-chan Result` says that callers consume the stream while the producer retains send-side lifecycle ownership. A sink accepting `chan<- Event` cannot inspect unrelated incoming values. These constraints make an incorrect close or send harder to express, although they do not solve cancellation or multi-sender ownership on their own.

sections.title: Narrow a bidirectional channel at boundaries
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[make chan int] --> B[Producer sees chan<- int]
  A --> C[Consumer sees <-chan int]
  B -- send 7 --> A
  A -- receive 7 --> C
  D[Compiler] -. rejects receive .-> B
  D -. rejects send .-> C
```

questions.question: What happens when a Go channel is nil, and when is that behavior useful?
questions.title: Nil channels and disabled select cases
questions.direct_answer: The zero value of a channel is `nil`. A send to or receive from a nil channel blocks forever, and closing a nil channel panics. This is usually an initialization bug, but assigning nil to a channel used in `select` can intentionally disable that case because a nil-channel operation is never ready.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the nil channel state and its controlled use in select loops.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing a nil channel with an open empty channel or a closed channel.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three channel states through operation readiness rather than memorized slogans.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A declared but uninitialized channel has the value `nil`.
Sending to nil blocks forever; receiving from nil also blocks forever.
A nil channel case in `select` can never be chosen.
Use nil deliberately only when its disabled-case meaning is clear and tested.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A channel variable has a zero value of `nil`. Unlike a non-nil unbuffered channel, it has no communication state that could ever pair a sender and receiver. Therefore a direct send or receive waits forever, and `close(nil)` panics. This often appears when a constructor forgot `make` or a channel field was optional but not checked.

A nil channel is different from a closed channel. A closed channel is immediately ready to receive any buffered values and then zero values with `ok == false`. A nil channel is never ready. That readiness difference makes nil useful inside `select`.

For example, a loop can set an input channel variable to nil after that input is exhausted. Its receive case is then disabled while other cases, such as another input or cancellation, can continue. The select does not choose the nil case and does not need an extra Boolean condition around every iteration.

I use this deliberately only in a small state machine where the transition is visible. Outside `select`, a nil send or receive is generally a deadlock bug. I also make sure at least one other select case can proceed or that cancellation remains available.

sections.title: Think in terms of readiness
sections.content:
Channel state determines which operations can proceed. An open unbuffered channel becomes ready when a matching operation exists. An open buffered channel can also be ready because its queue has room or data. A closed channel is always ready to receive after its buffered data drains. A nil channel is never ready to send or receive.

`select` considers only operations that can proceed. Replacing a channel variable with nil therefore removes that path from the current state without rebuilding the select statement. This technique is useful for merging optional inputs or stopping sends after a queue empties, but it becomes confusing when channel assignments are scattered across a large function.

sections.title: Nil, open, and closed channel states
sections.content:
| State | Send | Receive | Close |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nil | Blocks forever | Blocks forever | Panics |
| Open, unbuffered | Waits for receiver | Waits for sender | Succeeds once |
| Open, buffered | Proceeds if space exists | Proceeds if data exists | Succeeds once |
| Closed | Panics | Buffered data, then zero value and `false` | Panics again |

sections.title: Disable one select branch with nil
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var disabled <-chan string
    ready := make(chan string, 1)
    ready <- "ready path"

    select {
    case message := <-disabled:
        fmt.Println(message)
    case message := <-ready:
        fmt.Println(message)
    }
}
```
The nil-channel case can never proceed, so the deterministic output is `ready path`.
